key_claims: Interpersonal synchronization of neural and bodily signals significantly predicted listening engagement.
Neural interpersonal synchronization was the only measure that significantly predicted attention.
Attention is primarily driven by cognitive processes represented in the brain.
Listening engagement additionally involves affective processes that are more strongly reflected in bodily responses.
Different forms of interpersonal synchronization reflect distinct dimensions of the listening experience.
Interpersonal synchronization is a potential objective marker of listening engagement.
limitations: The study involved only thirty participants.
The study used a specific experimental setup with two simultaneous speech streams.
The findings are based on a single experiment and may not generalize to other contexts.
The study does not establish causality between interpersonal synchronization and listening engagement.
what_not_to_say: Interpersonal synchronization can be used as a clinical diagnostic tool.
The study proves that attention and listening engagement are completely independent.
The study provides specific numerical values for the strength of the predictions.
The study shows that bodily signals are more important than neural signals for attention.
